message.reasoning:
I'm planning JUnit 4 tests for TarArchiveOutputStream, mapping out the branch coverage needed for finish(), close(), and putArchiveEntry() including the long filename mode handling.

Continuing to trace branches through closeArchiveEntry() and write() for the assembly buffer logic and record boundary checks, and sketching out the test method names I'll need to cover constructors, setters, and record size defaults.

I'm also planning tests for finish/close behavior including double-close safety, plus a series of putArchiveEntry tests covering normal files, directories, and the three long-filename modes (ERROR, TRUNCATE, GNU) to hit each branch.

Then I'm outlining tests for closeArchiveEntry edge cases (zero-size entries, insufficient bytes written, and buffer flushing), and write() tests covering exceeding declared size and the assembly-buffer merge path when partial writes combine to fill a full record.

I still need tests for the case where the assembly buffer stays partial, writing exact multiples of record size to hit the full-record loop branch, writing partial remainders after the initial assembly buffer is empty, verifying flush() doesn't throw, and confirming createArchiveEntry returns a proper TarArchiveEntry. I'm also noting I need to double-check TarBuffer's default block and record sizes for these tests.

For the long file name test, I need to know NAMELEN's value (likely 100) and generate a name string longer than that, maybe repeating "a" 150 times. When longFileMode is GNU, the code creates a synthetic longLinkEntry with the fixed GNU longlink name and type, recursively calls putArchiveEntry on it (which won't trigger recursion again since that name is short), writes the long name bytes plus a null terminator, closes that entry, then proceeds to write the original entry's header normally -- so my test just needs to call putArchiveEntry with a long-named entry under GNU mode and verify this flow works.

I'll set the entry's size to 0 so I can skip writing data and just call closeArchiveEntry directly, avoiding complications with the write(int) vs write(byte[], int, int) overload behavior I was second-guessing.

Now I'm working out how to test the assembly buffer logic, particularly the branch where the accumulated length plus new bytes reaches the record buffer's full size (512 bytes by default), which triggers the full-write path.

The remaining 502 bytes fill the record, currBytes updates, and the leftover 98 bytes get buffered into assemBuf for the next round. Then when closing the archive entry, since assemLen is nonzero, I pad the rest with zeroes and write the final record.

Good, matches total. Now checking the other branch where assemLen stays partial after two small writes—first write of 10 bytes then a second write of 5 bytes keeps the combined 15 bytes under the record size, so it just accumulates in the buffer without triggering a full record write.

For the case where a write exactly fills a full 512-byte record with no prior partial data, the code skips the leftover-copy step and goes straight into the write loop, which writes the record directly since the remaining bytes exactly equal the record size, bringing total bytes written to 512—matching expectations on close.

I also want to verify behavior when writing more than one full record at once.

I need to test writing when the requested size exceeds the entry's declared size, expecting an exception. I also want to check that closing an entry without writing anything when a nonzero size was declared throws an IOException, and that calling finish() with an entry still open also throws for unclosed entries. Finally, I want to confirm that calling close() twice is safe, with the second call simply being a no-op.

For the actual test code, I'll need to figure out whether TarConstants values like NAMELEN are accessible from the same package, and just pick a string length like 200 characters for a name field test to exercise truncation or overflow behavior.

Writing the createLongName helper...

Now I'll draft the full JUnit4 test file, including a test for createArchiveEntry(File, String) that creates a temp file and checks the returned entry's type, name, and size match expectations.

For exception scenarios I'll use @Test(expected=IOException.class) rather than manual try/catch blocks. I'm also confirming that write(byte[]) doesn't need explicit overriding since the base OutputStream class already delegates to write(b, 0, b.length), which correctly routes to the overridden method.

Now I'm double-checking whether write(int b) is actually implemented somewhere in the class hierarchy, since OutputStream declares it abstract and this class only overrides write(byte[], off, len) -- I need to verify ArchiveOutputStream provides a concrete implementation for single-byte writes.

I'll finalize the test code, checking that TarBuffer's default record size is accessible and deciding whether to hardcode the expected 512 value or reference the constant directly for the assertion.

Actually, to avoid depending on exact default record size values, I should construct TarArchiveOutputStream with explicit recordSize parameters throughout the tests -- maybe using a simple round number like 100 to keep the math easy for the write-related tests.

With recordSize=100, I trace through the exact-record and multi-record write scenarios: writing exactly 100 bytes fills one record cleanly, while writing 250 bytes fills two full records and leaves 50 bytes buffered in the assembly buffer, verifying currBytes and currSize update correctly at each step.

I then check the merge case where a partial 30-byte assembly buffer combines with a subsequent 90-byte write to complete a record (30+90=120 spans exactly one record boundary), confirming the copy logic splits data properly between assemBuf and the new write buffer, leaving 20 bytes still pending. I also verify a case where two partial writes (30+40=70) never reach a full record and simply accumulate in the assembly buffer without triggering the write loop, with closeArchiveEntry correctly flushing the remainder in both cases.

Now I'm considering edge cases: writing data that exceeds the declared entry size should throw immediately before any assembly logic runs, and calling closeArchiveEntry when currBytes is less than the declared currSize (no data written at all) should also throw. For directory entries, I'm reasoning that size gets forced to zero regardless of what was set, so putArchiveEntry followed immediately by closeArchiveEntry should succeed with no writes attempted, since any write would fail against a zero size. I'm also noting the TarArchiveEntry constructor likely infers directory status from a trailing slash in the name.

For the GNU long name case, I'm testing that a zero-size entry with a long name correctly triggers the internal long-link sub-entry handling (writing its own header and data, closing it) before falling through to write the actual entry's header, after which closeArchiveEntry succeeds trivially since both currSize and currBytes are zero. I'm now setting up a separate test for LONGFILE_TRUNCATE mode with a long-named, zero-size entry, verifying that putArchiveEntry doesn't throw and proceeds through normal handling instead of hitting the failure branch for oversized names.

Adding the default LONGFILE_ERROR case, which should throw a RuntimeException when a name exceeds the length limit and no truncate/GNU mode is set. I'm also drafting tests for finish() with an unclosed entry (expects an IOException), finish() with no entries at all (should succeed silently), calling close() twice in a row (second call should be a harmless no-op), and calling flush() on the stream (should not throw). Finally I'm starting a createArchiveEntry test using a temp file.
